extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners preparing or prosecuting U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and examiner guidance from the MPEP (Chapter 1500) governing what constitutes a patentable ornamental design and how to prepare, examine, and prosecute U.S. design patent applications (specification, drawings, claim, formalities, and related procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes and Rules Applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are governed by 35 U.S.C. 171 and related provisions; 37 CFR 1.151 and 37 CFR 1.152-1.155 set forth rules specific to design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patent applications are not included in the PCT; unless otherwise noted, other MPEP chapters/rules for utility patents apply to design cases. Cite specific statutes/regulations (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 171; 37 CFR 1.151, 1.152-1.155) when making procedural or substantive determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Design
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed subject matter is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture — i.e., the visual characteristics/appearance presented to the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design may concern configuration (shape), surface ornamentation, or both. A design is inseparable from the article, must be definite and preconceived, capable of reproduction, and not merely the chance result of a method. Case law (e.g., In re Zahn) supports these points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality Requirement / Statutory Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 171 requires a new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture; subject matter must be ornamental, not purely functional or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design claims that are merely functional or derogatory/offensive may be rejected as improper subject matter. Ornamentality is judged from the appearance; functional/structural features are not considered part of design patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Design and Utility Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect appearance; utility patents protect function/workings. Many procedural and substantive differences exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key differences to consider include: term (14 years from grant for design vs 20 years from filing for utility), no maintenance fees for designs, single claim only in design, mandatory restriction practice in designs, no PCT coverage for designs, foreign priority period (6 months for designs v. 1 year for utility provisional), no provisional benefit for designs, RCE unavailable for designs, CPA practice and publication differences. Use this list to determine applicable practices and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a Design Patent Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A design application must include the arrangement and elements set forth in 37 CFR 1.154: transmittal form, fee form, application data sheet, specification, drawings/photographs, and executed oath/declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim in proper form and an adequate drawing or photograph are essential elements. Follow the order and section headings recommended in 37 CFR 1.154 and the MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification — Title and Preamble Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title must designate the particular article; preamble may state applicant name, title of design, and brief description of nature and intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title must correspond to the claim; if title and claim do not correspond, object under 37 CFR 1.153. Titles must not be directed to less than the claimed design shown in full lines. Titles describing combinations or multiple parts must clearly define them as a single entity (e.g., 'set', 'pair', 'assembly'). Amendments to the title must have antecedent basis and not introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification — Figure Descriptions and Descriptive Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief description of the drawing figures is ordinarily sufficient; additional descriptive statements are permissible in limited forms but generally not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible statements (if present in the original filing) include: description of unillustrated portions, disclaimers of portions not claimed, statements explaining broken lines, statement of nature/intented use, and a 'characteristic features' statement. Descriptive matter added after filing that constitutes new matter is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible Specification Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain descriptive statements are not allowed in the specification of an issued design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers directed at portions shown in solid lines, descriptions suggesting other unillustrated embodiments (except mirror images or obvious variants), or statements directed to function/structure (rather than appearance) are impermissible and should be removed or objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic Feature Statement — Use and Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may include a 'characteristic feature' statement identifying a feature considered novel, but this does not determine patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If used, phrase as 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [ ... ]'. Such statements may later serve to limit claims but examiners must assess patentability based on the overall appearance, not only the stated feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Claim Form and Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications may include only a single claim, which should be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article 'as shown' or 'as shown and described' (if descriptive matter is in the specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim language must correspond to the title and be consistent with specification terminology. The claim defines the subject matter the applicant regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph). Examiners should permit reasonable latitude in claim language but object if language is clearly misdescriptive or indefinitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Lines vs Broken Lines in Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Full (solid) lines show the claimed design; broken lines can show environment or boundaries but may not be used to denote portions of lesser importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken lines may illustrate environment or indicate bounds of a claim; they may not show hidden planes/surfaces not visible through opaque materials, nor be used to claim that parts are immaterial. Where broken lines are used for multiple purposes, the specification must explicitly state their purpose(s). Addition of certain broken-line boundaries may be new matter if not clearly derivable from the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing Requirement and Centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing or photograph is an essential element of a design application and constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the design; it must be clear and complete so nothing is left to conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings must comply with 37 CFR 1.84 and 1.152 and include sufficient views to disclose the complete appearance. Inconsistencies among views should be objected to; severe inconsistencies may render the claim nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Views — Number and Type Required
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings should contain sufficient views (front, rear, top, bottom, sides) to disclose the complete appearance; perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit duplicative or flat views if the specification explicitly states why they are omitted (e.g., sides identical or mirror images). Sectional views solely showing internal/functional construction are unnecessary and may confuse scope; include sectional views only to clarify exterior contour when needed and only with antecedent basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface Shading Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate and adequate surface shading should be used to show character/contour of surfaces of three-dimensional aspects; surface shading is important to distinguish open and solid areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface shading is not required in every case but lack of necessary shading may render a design nonenabling/indefinite. Solid black shading is only permitted to represent the color black (or color contrast). Use oblique line shading for transparent/reflective surfaces; use line shading and stippling to indicate material/contrast without limiting to particular materials or colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs in Lieu of Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs are permitted only under restrictions and must not disclose environmental structure; photographs and ink drawings may not be combined on the same formal submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs must be limited to the claimed design and avoid showing environment. Mixing media (photograph + ink drawing) on the same formal drawing is prohibited. If photographs are used, ensure they comply with 37 CFR 1.152 and do not create ambiguity about claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken-line Boundary Additions and New Matter Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding broken-line boundaries that are not straight or that otherwise differ from the original showing may constitute new matter and be prohibited under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a straight broken-line boundary is clear from the original disclosure (e.g., connecting ends of existing full lines), applicant may amend to add it; other broken-line changes require caution to avoid new matter. Examiners should ensure any added broken-line boundaries have clear antecedent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of New Matter When Amending Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Any corrected or new drawings filed after the original must avoid introducing new matter; replacement sheets must include all figures present on the prior version even if only one figure is amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotated marked-up copies showing canceled/changed figures should be provided. If all figures on a sheet are canceled, a replacement sheet is not required but an annotated sheet is. Care must be exercised in preparing replacement drawings to avoid 35 U.S.C. 132 problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing Corrections Prior to Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Outstanding drawing deficiencies must be corrected before an appeal of the design claim proceeds; appeals without corrected drawings may be dismissed or denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph language requiring corrected drawings in reply to Office action to avoid abandonment. Final rejections may include direction that drawings be corrected prior to appeal (Ex parte Bevan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity for Good Drawings — Enablement and Filing Date Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the drawing is the whole disclosure, good drawings are critical; insufficient drawings may be fatal to validity and can adversely affect effective filing date of continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should require appropriate shading, sufficient views, and consistency. Insufficient drawings can trigger 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections (first paragraph — nonenablement) and definite claims under 112 second paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction — Overall Appearance Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability (novelty/nonobviousness) of a design is judged on the overall visual appearance of the claimed design as compared to prior art, not on individual functional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic feature statements notwithstanding, the examiner must compare total appearance to prior art (see In re Rosen, In re Leslie). Rejections for novelty/nonobviousness should be framed in terms of overall appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory Restriction Practice in Design Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction between plural, distinct inventions embodied in the same design application is mandatory (see MPEP § 1504.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple patentably distinct embodiments are disclosed in the drawings, require an election; failure to elect may pause examination and restriction requirements must be followed. Divisional applications for nonelected inventions must meet their own expedited or filing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and Benefit Rules Specific to Designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications have distinct priority/benefit rules: foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) is 6 months for designs; design applications may not claim benefit of a provisional under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of shorter priority periods for designs versus utility applications and the unavailability of provisional/1-year benefit provisions for design filings. The PCT does not apply to design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited Examination Under 37 CFR 1.155
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request expedited examination under 37 CFR 1.155; such requests result in assignment and prioritized processing if all criteria are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expedited requests should be filed with a complete application; incomplete applications will not be examined even if expedited is requested. If requirements are unmet, applicant is notified and given a shortened period to comply; expedited status is subject to conditions (does not automatically carry to divisionals unless they meet requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance, Term, and Reissue Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are granted for a term of 14 years from the date of grant; reissue practice exists but the term may not be extended by reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue applications must follow Chapter 1400 practices; changes to drawings in reissue have special procedural requirements (explain all changes on separate sheets; submit annotated marked-up drawings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship with Copyright and Trademark
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent protection may overlap with copyright and trademark protection; an author/inventor may secure both copyright and design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of a copyright notice in a design application is permitted under conditions: notice placement, limited content (e.g., '© 1983 John Doe'), a waiver paragraph reserving reproduction rights must be included in the specification. Trademarks may be included in drawings under limited circumstances; trademarks should not be used alone in the title and derogatory use of a trademark will cause rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Copyright Notice — Formatting and Waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright notice may be placed adjacent to copyright material in the application (including drawings) but must conform to size and wording limits and must be accompanied by a waiver statement in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If placed on a drawing, print size must be 1/8 to 1/4 inch and within sight of the drawing. The specification must include the waiver language that the copyright owner 'has no objection to the facsimile reproduction by anyone of the patent document ...' else the notice will be objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Trademarks in Design Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks may be used in specifications/drawings only under limited circumstances; use in the title is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If trademark material forms part of a claimed design drawing, include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material and the owner. Examiners should object to trademarks in the title and require deletion. Derogatory uses of trademarks may result in rejection as offensive subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Functional/Structural Descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications must focus on ornamental appearance; functional or structural matter is not permitted or relevant in design patent specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements describing function, operation, or mechanical/internal structure should be excluded as they are unrelated to design patentability. Emphasize and enforce the ornamental/visual scope when reviewing specification and drawings.
